summary: Describes how some fields of DHCP messages should be used on IEEE 1394 (FireWire) networks, because its link-layer addressing differs from Ethernet. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: FireWire cables label devices differently than Ethernet does. This explains how the automatic address-giving service should fill in its forms so it works on FireWire.

questions: how to configure firewire devices with dhcp
subtitle: Clarifies how DHCP works over IEEE 1394 (FireWire) networks

tldr.problem: IEEE 1394 (FireWire) uses different link-layer addressing than Ethernet, so some DHCP message fields must be clarified for interoperability on 1394 networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies that htype must be 24, hlen must be 0, the chaddr field is reserved and ignored, and clients must use the BROADCAST flag and the client identifier option with EUI-64 IDs.
tldr.outcome: Enables DHCP to work correctly on IEEE 1394 networks by adapting to the FireWire protocol's addressing model rather than traditional Ethernet.

today: RFC 2855 is a Proposed Standard that specifies DHCP usage on IEEE 1394 networks. It remains published and is used by 1394 implementations that need DHCP configuration.

sections.title: DHCP Over FireWire
sections.content:
IEEE Standard 1394-1995 defines the High Performance Serial Bus, commonly known as FireWire. The IETF IP1394 Working Group standardized how to carry IPv4 datagrams and 1394 ARP packets over IEEE 1394 networks.

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network. However, 1394 uses a different link-layer addressing method than conventional Ethernet and other IEEE 802 networks, so some DHCP field usage must be clarified to ensure interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: FireWire is a way to send data over cables. Unlike regular network cables, FireWire names devices differently, so the automatic address setup needs different rules for it.

sections.title: 1394-Specific DHCP Field Usage
sections.content:
The htype (hardware address type) field MUST be set to 24 for 1394. The hlen (hardware address length) MUST be 0 because 1394 node IDs are transient and will not be consistent across 1394 bridges, so the RFC recommends not putting them in the chaddr field.

The chaddr (client hardware address) field is reserved: senders must set it to zero and recipients must ignore its value. Instead, clients MUST use the client identifier option (option 61), which may consist of any data. Since every IP over 1394 node has an EUI-64 (node unique ID), the RFC recommends using EUI-64 as the client identifier. A DHCP client should request broadcast replies by setting the BROADCAST flag in DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages when 1394 ARP is not yet available.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally DHCP fills in a computer's hardware address so replies can reach it. FireWire addresses do not work that way, so instead each device includes a unique ID number in its request, and the server sends back a broadcast message that everyone can hear.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: DHCP currently provides no authentication or security mechanisms; security exposures are discussed in the DHCP protocol specification. On 1394 networks, a malicious client can falsify its EUI-64 identifier and masquerade as another client, since there is no built-in verification mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the network could pretend to be a different device, since there is no way to verify that the ID number they claim is really theirs.
